title: A Lady’s Refinement
mood: A girl in a great house learns to count to three, and to wait outside a closed door.

hero.alt: The dark outline of a tall man in a fur-collared greatcoat, a scroll in one hand, a gold question mark glowing on his chest.

segs.t: The first person who ever counted for her was Hester.
Guinevere was small then. She ran down the garden stair too fast, caught her toe and landed on both knees on the stone. One knee bled.
A woman in a gray coat knelt on the step below her. It was Hester, of the House’s guard, who never laughed.
“Up, miss,” said Hester. “One. Two. Three.”
Guinevere stood on three. Then she laughed loud enough for both of them. Hester did not smile.
After that, Hester counted three at every fall. Soon Guinevere counted with her.
It was the first thing Guinevere could place. Under it lay something older: candlelight, and a voice counting in the dark. She could not put it anywhere.
She found out where it came from when she was small enough to ask anything. It was bedtime. Her door stood open, and Hester stood in it.
“Who’s the lady in the long hall?” asked Guinevere. “In the picture.”
“Your mother, miss.”
“Where is she?”
Hester was quiet a moment. Then she told it the way she gave a report.
“There was a storm one night. After midnight, every lamp in the House went out at once. Everything that ran on current died with them.”
“Even the sirens?”
“Even the sirens. There was only rain and thunder, and a violet light at the edges of the shutters.”
“Were you scared?”
“I was the newest guard in the House. I carried you down to the cellar with one candle. I counted the steps out loud, so you would not cry.”
“Did I cry?”
“No, miss.”
Guinevere lay still.
The voice in the dark,
she thought.
That was Hester.
“And my mother?”
“Your mother was down in the city that night, at the House’s bank by the harbor. She was working late.” Hester’s voice did not change. “She did not come home.”
“Oh.”
“At dawn I stood at the end of the long hall with you asleep on my shoulder. Your father stood in the door of his office a long time. Then he shut it.”
Guinevere waited for the rest.
“Go to sleep, miss.”
Hester left the door open. Guinevere lay listening to her footsteps go down the corridor, stop, and come back.
Hester never told it again. From that night on, Guinevere slept with her door open.
The first morning her hair was long enough, Hester stood behind her at the mirror and tied two red bows in it. Hester had kept them back when the House cleared her mother’s rooms.
“Whose are they?”
“Your mother’s, miss. From her dressing table.”
Guinevere touched them with both hands. After that she tied them herself, and nobody else touched them.

House Baroque was one of the great money houses of Terrinia. It lent the city money for the Energy System that powered the dome, and for rebuilding each ward after a raid. A board of the House’s elders and partners ran it. Her father held the head seat.
He put a detail of guards around his daughter, with Hester, who had carried her down the cellar steps, at its head. Guinevere never left the House without them.
He had lost his wife to the Enders. Money bought walls, so money was safety. Guinevere worked that out years later. He never said a word of it.
She ate at one end of the long table in the dining room. His chair at the far end stood empty most nights. He spoke to her through his office door. Nobody went in there until he called.
The first page of sums she ever finished, she took to him herself. His door off the long hall stood half open. She held the page up to the gap.
“Father, I finished my accounts.”
A hand in a dark sleeve took it. A pen scratched. The page came back with a red mark on line four.
“Again.”
She did it again on the bench outside, her tongue between her teeth. Her feet did not reach the floor.
“Sit up,” said the voice behind the door.
She sat up. The second time the page did not come back.
He kept it,
she thought.
“Tomorrow, accounts.”
She stayed on the bench a while, in case there was more. There was not.
On his birthday she had the kitchen bake a cake and carried it to that bench herself. In the morning the plate was on the bench again, washed.
Tutors came: accounts, contracts, manners. The manners tutor talked all day about “a lady’s refinement.” She meant how you held your back.
Guinevere glued the tutor’s words to Hester’s count. The next time she fell, on the terrace steps, she was up before Hester reached her.
“A lady’s refinement,” she announced. “Three seconds.”
Hester counted anyway.

The guards were her only company. They played hide and seek with her and always won, because finding her was their job. The guards got cakes too. She carried each one out to the gate herself. Hester ate hers standing up.
The guards never came into the long hall. It was the master’s. The detail stopped at a chair where the hall began, and nobody ever sat in it.
Years later she ran down that hall and her heel slid on the marble. She went down hard under her mother’s portrait.
Nobody came. Behind his door, a pen kept scratching.
She got up on her own. “One,” she said. “Two. Three.”
Her voice went down the marble, and nothing answered it. Her knee stung. She kept her chin up until the lamp under the portrait stopped blurring.

At dawn the guards drilled in the yard. Guinevere watched from the steps and pestered Hester every morning. Hester had learned to fight from an old Shield sergeant, before the House hired her. One dawn, she gave in.
“Elbow in,” said Hester. “Hip first. Hands home after every punch.”
Guinevere hit the sandbag. It hardly swung. Her wrist hurt.
“Hands home,” said Hester.
Guinevere brought them home and hit it again. After that she punched the sandbag every dawn, before her lessons.

When she was older still, a chair was set for her at the back of the board’s long room. From there she saw only the top of her father’s chair at the head of the table, a fur collar over it, and one hand on the papers.
The board talked in numbers. A loan for the dome. A loan for a ward rebuilt after a raid. Guinevere counted the people inside the numbers. A ward was streets. Streets were families.
At one meeting her father turned a page and spoke to the table. “My daughter takes a junior seat when she comes of age. This seat, after me.”
Nobody looked back at her chair. It was arranged. She was the heir.
She sat on her hands.
It’s his table and his money,
she thought.
Nothing in this room is mine.
Then, one bright morning, the guards shouted in the yard.
Guinevere ran out onto the terrace. She looked back once. Hester was behind her.
Figures were crossing the sky above the hill, high and fast, on wings of light. They flew over the city in a line and turned toward the water.
“That,” said Guinevere. She pointed with her whole arm.
By evening the House knew what they were. A new school had opened its gate that day: Selrick Academy. Its instructors were Shield soldiers, and they had flown its first finished suits over the city.
Soon the Academy announced its first entrance assessment. It would test children her age for aspirant power. Nobody could buy a pass.
Money can’t buy those wings,
she thought.
Not even his. If I win them, they’re mine.
She told her father through the office door.
“I’m going to sit the Academy’s entrance assessment.”
Silence. A page turned.
“You will be home within the year.”
That was all. He did not forbid it.
The Academy has walls of its own,
she thought.
Better ones than ours. He’s done the sums. He thinks I’ll fail, or get bored.
She stood at the door a while longer. He would not make a bargain out loud, so she made one with him in her head.
If I come first, with none of your money, you’ll have to see.
Then he would say the sentence she had never heard.
Well done, Guinevere.
The morning of the entrance assessment.
Hester drove her across the city. Through the back window the House sat on its hill and grew smaller.
The car stopped at the Academy gate. Children were going in with bags over their shoulders. The detail could not follow her inside. The Academy guarded itself.
Guinevere climbed out and touched her two red bows. “Wait here.”
Hester’s face did not move. “Yes, miss.”
Guinevere walked in with her chin up. Her hands were cold. She did not look back. A black-haired girl with a cloth bag went past her, eyes front.

Behind them an Academy guard swung the gate shut after the last child. At the clang, Guinevere turned. Through the bars she saw Hester beside the car in her gray coat, where she had been told to wait.
